title: Who's lying?: use redundant, differently-built data sources to catch bad metrics
summary: Using a pilot's lesson (stuck fuel gauges, checked with a wooden stick), Jason argues that important business metrics must be derived two different ways, because some data is always lying. Redundancy catches errors and also gives a fuller picture of what is driving the numbers.

principles.text: Redundancy must be differently implemented, not just duplicated; two things sharing a failure mode fail together.
principles.quote: It's not even good enough to just have "two of everything." If two things both rely on electricity, and the electricity goes out, you lose both.

principles.text: Always ask 'Who's lying?' about your metrics: usually they're right, but sometimes one is wrong and you won't know.
principles.quote: Usually your instruments are correct, but sometimes one is lying.

principles.text: Cross-check key numbers across independent systems, such as billing vs bank, Stripe vs your user portal, analytics vs raw logs.
principles.quote: Revenue from your billing system compared to cash flows from your bank statements.

principles.text: Data errors come from mundane causes: formula bugs, missing tracking code, unsent surveys, bad query filters, dead update scripts.
principles.quote: The spreadsheet had a subtle bug in a formula, the analytics JavaScript code was accidentally left off one page, the survey email didn't get sent to all the customers in the cohort

principles.text: Computing the same data multiple ways also improves understanding of the forces behind it; biased sources partly cancel when combined.
principles.quote: None has the full picture; all are biased. But taken together, your picture of the world is more complete, and biases might be cancelled through averaging

principles.text: Any metric watched daily and acted on deserves a second, independent check for accuracy and comprehension.
principles.quote: If a metric is important enough to watch it every day, and to act if its behavior deviates from expectation, then it's important enough to be double-checked.
